newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian premier asks what went wrong with economy.
newsitem.headline: Indian premier asks what went wrong with economy.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Wednesday deplored the state of the economy, saying something must be wrong if communist China can attract more foreign investment than democratic India.

In a frank, off-the-cuff speech to the captains of industry, Deve Gowda repeatedly appealed for concrete advice on how to spur economic growth while bringing down interest rates and controlling red ink.
"Where did things go wrong?" he asked in a candid admission of frustration over the economy.
Pressure has been building on Deve Gowda's 4-1/2 month old coalition government to stimulate economic growth.
Recent economic indicators reflect slower growth of industrial production and exports, and rising inflation.
Annual interest rates for top-rated borrowers range from 15.5 to 19.0 percent, while inflation as measured by the wholesale price index was at 6.34 percent in September.
Many analysts do not expect the government to meet its target of seven percent growth in gross domestic product in the fiscal year that began on April 1.
The prospect of slower than expected growth has contributed to a share selloff since Deve Gowda took office in June.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark index has lost nearly a quarter of its value since touching an intraday year high of 4,131.22 points on June 17. On Tuesday the index closed at 3,118.95 points.
"Why today are interest rates so high?" Deve Gowda asked the annual meeting of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India.
"Give me a concrete suggestion how to bring down interest rates and what steps to take to attract investment."

Deve Gowda openly lamented what he called India's lack of technology and inefficient manufacturing, and said the nation had fallen short of its economic goals during five years of liberalisation under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
"What exactly is the reason we are not achieving our expected results?" he asked, saying one in three Indians still lived below the poverty line.
The leader of India's centre-left government asked why China was attracting so much more foreign investment than India, which began opening its doors to outside investment and trade in 1991.
In 1994, China pulled in $33.8 billion of foreign direct investment compared to India's $620 million, according to the World Bank.

"China is a communist country, India is the largest democratic country," Deve Gowda said. "Why is India unable to get the expected investment and China is able to get it? What exactly is the drawback in our system?"
The prime minister assured foreign investors that India's democracy was stable, and he reiterated that the five-year-old economic liberalisation programme was irreversible.
"If they are really interested in investing in this country, let them not have any kind of confusion or suspicion in their mind," he said.

But he said India must not depend only on foreign investment, and appealed to domestic firms to put more money into India. "Those with the capacity to invest, they try to think of other countries for their investment," he said.
"Why not India?"
